title: On Bit-level Reverse Engineering of Vehicular CAN Bus
problem: CAN bus reverse engineering struggles to achieve bit-level resolution of signal-to-action mappings due to massive search space over unique IDs and payload combinations. Security vulnerability assessment requires precise bit-level identification.
motivation: Vehicle cybersecurity depends on identifying which bits in CAN messages control specific functions; current methods lack the precision and resource efficiency needed for practical deployment on edge devices like Raspberry Pi.
method: The technique breaks down CAN bus messages—the signals vehicles use to control functions like acceleration and steering—by systematically testing which individual bits trigger which car actions. It does this through bit-level signal extraction (isolating the specific control bits that matter) combined with exhaustive mapping (systematically checking every bit pattern combination against observed vehicle behavior). The researchers validated the approach on a Tesla Model 3 and Leapmotor C10/C11 vehicles, and demonstrated it runs efficiently enough on a Raspberry Pi.
key_novelty: It shows how to precisely identify which individual bits in vehicle control messages trigger which actions, using minimal computing power—efficient enough to run on inexpensive hardware like a Raspberry Pi.
contributions: Systematic framework for bit-level CAN message reverse engineering
Successfully identified 43 distinct car-control actions on Tesla Model 3
Demonstrated portability across multiple vehicle platforms (Tesla, Leapmotor)
Lightweight implementation suitable for embedded systems (Raspberry Pi)
limitations: Evaluation focused on three vehicle models; generalization to other OEMs and CAN protocol variants not discussed.
primary_theme: Automotive CAN bus security analysis via bit-level reverse engineering
